item.title: Gunkanjima (Battleship Island) — Guide
item.description: Gunkanjima, officially Hashima, is a small abandoned island off Nagasaki whose silhouette of dense high-rise ruins resembles a battleship — hence its nickname. From the 1880s it was a coal-mining island, and to house the thousands of miners and their families, some of Japan’s first large reinforced-concrete apartment blocks were packed onto its tiny surface, making it at its peak in the 1950s the most densely populated place on Earth. When the mine closed in 1974 everyone left almost overnight, and the island was frozen in time — a ghostly maze of decaying buildings, empty stairwells and shattered windows slowly reclaimed by the sea and weather.

item.title: Hirosaka Castle Ruins: A Quiet Hilltop in Izumo — Guide
item.description: Hirosaka Castle is a ruined mountain castle in the Izumo area, the kind of quiet historical site that rewards travellers who prefer atmosphere and imagination to reconstructed keeps. Little remains above ground beyond earthworks, terraced platforms and traces of stone, worn by centuries and half-reclaimed by trees, but the outline of the old fortifications can still be read across the hilltop, and the climb is rewarded with a view over the Izumo plain.

item.title: Katsuren Castle Ruins — Guide
item.description: Katsuren Castle (Katsuren-jo), on a hill on the Katsuren Peninsula in central Okinawa, is one of the island’s oldest gusuku (Ryukyu castles) and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, famous for its commanding hilltop position and superb panoramic views. Dating to around the 13th–14th centuries, it was the seat of the powerful and ambitious lord Amawari, whose prosperity through overseas trade made Katsuren a thriving centre — a history dramatically underlined in 2016 when archaeologists discovered ancient Roman and Ottoman coins among the ruins, hinting at the reach of Ryukyu’s trade networks.

item.title: Mihara Castle & the Suigun Road: A Sea-Castle Ruin — Guide
item.description: Mihara Castle was built in the 1560s by Kobayakawa Takakage on islets in the sea, a naval stronghold so surrounded by water it was nicknamed the ‘floating castle’. Land reclamation has long since left it inland, and its keep is gone, but substantial stone ramparts and a moat survive — remarkably, right against Mihara’s shinkansen station, whose platforms were built over part of the site, making this possibly the most accessible castle ruin in Japan.

item.title: Nakagusuku Castle Ruins — Guide
item.description: Nakagusuku Castle (Nakagusuku-jo) is one of the best-preserved of Okinawa’s gusuku (Ryukyu castles) and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, spread across a ridge in central Okinawa with commanding views. Built in stages up to the 15th century and associated with the renowned lord Gosamaru, the castle is celebrated for the beauty and sophistication of its curving limestone walls, which sweep gracefully along the contours of the hilltop and showcase several styles of Ryukyuan stone-fitting technique.

item.title: Nakijin Castle Ruins — Guide
item.description: Nakijin Castle (Nakijin-jo), on the Motobu Peninsula in northern Okinawa, is one of the island’s largest and most impressive gusuku (Ryukyu castle) ruins and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Once the stronghold of the kings of Hokuzan, one of the three kingdoms that divided Okinawa before its 15th-century unification, the castle sprawls across a scenic hilltop, its long, undulating stone walls winding for hundreds of metres along the ridgeline and commanding sweeping views over the surrounding forest and the sea.

item.title: Taketa & Oka Castle Ruins — Guide
item.description: The ruins of Oka Castle (Oka-jō), above the town of Taketa in inland Oita, are among the most spectacular and atmospheric castle ruins in Japan. Built on a natural rock plateau high on a steep ridge, this formidable mountaintop fortress once controlled the region, but its buildings were demolished in the Meiji era, leaving only the vast, sweeping stone walls and ramparts perched dramatically along the clifftops. Walking the ruins today, with panoramic views over the surrounding mountains and the Kuju range — especially stunning wreathed in autumn colours or a sea of clouds — is a moving experience.

item.title: Tottori Castle Ruins: Stone Walls Above the City — Guide
item.description: Tottori Castle was a mountain stronghold on Kyusho Hill above the city, remembered above all for the terrible siege of 1581, when the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi surrounded and starved the castle into surrender in one of the most brutal blockades of Japan’s warring-states era. The keep is long gone, but extensive stone ramparts survive on the hill and around its base, along with a reconstructed gate and, unusually, the stone-built base of a Meiji-era Western-style building.

item.title: Ryukyu Gusuku Guide: Zakimi Castle & UNESCO Ruins
item.description: Long before Shuri unified the islands, Okinawa was dotted with gusuku — the fortified castles of rival Ryukyu lords. Several of their dramatic ruins, prized for their flowing, beautifully engineered curved limestone walls, are inscribed together as UNESCO World Heritage (“Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu”). Zakimi Castle in Yomitan is among the most accessible and best preserved, its ramparts open to walk and offering views to the sea.
